newsitem.title: USA: INSIGHT -- Upside tests beckon to dollar/yen.
newsitem.headline: INSIGHT -- Upside tests beckon to dollar/yen.

text.p: The dollar broke out of a two-month triangle pattern when it soared above 124.82 yen, said chartists who predicted the U.S. currency rally has not run out of steam yet.
During Asian trade on Monday, the greenback hurled past 124.82 yen, a level it first hit on February 14.
"It was a signal we made new highs and everybody followed through with it," said Scott Siller, a senior technical analyst at MCM CurrencyWatch.
Siller pegged the dollar's next upside objective at 126.25 yen, a peak from January 1993.
Beyond 126.25 yen, Siller sketched another dollar target at 127.75 yen, a level he described as a two-month bull channel projection.

When U.S. trading got under way on Monday, the dollar climbed further, briefly touching a fresh 50-month peak of 125.81 yen. At 1500 EDT/1900 GMT, the greenback was at 125.50/60 yen, barely changed from 125.50/55 yen at the open.

As for a somewhat longer-term upside target, Ken Boyer, a senior currency strategist at MMS International, pointed to 129.60 yen, a 61.8 percent Fibonacci retracement of the major downtrend from April 1990 through April 1995.
The dollar had tumbled to a post-World War II low of 79.75 yen on April 19, 1995. The rally to 125.81 yen represents nearly a 58 percent appreciation in the value of the dollar.
On Monday, the U.S. unit also racked up impressive gains against the mark, briefly reaching 1.7133 marks in Europe.
Siller noted that the dollar rally on Monday pushed the daily indicators into positive territory.

The weekly indicators for dollar/mark have been bullish for a while, according to Siller. "They are a bit overbought but that can run for a while," he said, referring to the overbought condition of the weekly indicators.
The rally on Monday failed to lift the dollar to 1.7210 marks, its most recent high from March 7. At 1500 EDT/1900 GMT, the dollar stood at 1.7092/02 marks, up from 1.7030/35 marks at the open.
Chartists warned the dollar is vulnerable to a near-term correction versus the mark.
"We did have this real sharp jump higher (and) we're kind of vulnerable to pullbacks below 1.69 (marks) before people here get really excited about buying it again," Boyer said.
